name: shale
phi0_source: literature: Sclater & Christie (1980) JGR 85; same built-in value as lithology.py
phi_r_source: literature: residual shale porosity after mechanical compaction (typical basin-modelling floor; not measured here)
beta_1_MPa_source: assumed: chosen so the Schneider exponential roughly tracks the Sclater & Christie (1980) Athy shale curve near 2 km under hydrostatic load
grain_size_m_source: assumed: clay/silt scale (~2 μm); used only if a shale end-member is evaluated with Kozeny-Carman. Mudstone permeability uses Yang & Aplin (2010) instead
f_quartz_source: literature: typical quartz-silt fraction of North Sea mudstones (not point-counted at this well)
f_clay_source: literature: Yang & Aplin (2010) CF is mass fraction < 2 μm; 0.60 is a typical marine mudstone prior (not measured here)
coat_source: assumed: most quartz silt surfaces in mudstone are clay-coated so quartz cement is minor
friction_deg_source: literature: typical residual friction angle for mudstone (geotechnical range; not measured here)
kc_factor_source: literature: Carman (1937) spherical-grain constant (not used for shale permeability)
note: Mechanical plus minor quartz only. Smectite-to-illite and clay diagenesis are not in phase 1.

name: sandstone
phi0_source: literature: Sclater & Christie (1980) JGR 85; same built-in value as lithology.py
phi_r_source: literature: rigid-grain IGV floor ~26% (Paxton et al. 2002 AAPG Bull. 86; Lander & Walderhaug 1999 AAPG Bull. 83)
beta_1_MPa_source: assumed: chosen so IGV approaches the 26% floor by ~2.5 km / ~30 MPa hydrostatic load (Paxton et al. 2002); not inverted from this well
grain_size_m_source: assumed: typical fine-to-medium sand d50 (0.25 ± 0.10 mm). Beard & Weyl (1973) AAPG Bull. 57 texture scale; not a grain-size analysis of this well
f_quartz_source: assumed: quartzose sandstone prior (typical detrital quartz fraction); not a thin-section point count from this well
f_clay_source: assumed: small clay-size fraction in a clean-to-moderately clayey sandstone (not measured here)
coat_source: assumed: partial illite/chlorite grain coatings are common in North Sea sands (Ehrenberg 1993 AAPG Bull. 77) but the 0.30 value is not measured at this well
friction_deg_source: literature: typical residual friction angle for sandstone (geotechnical range; not measured here)
note: Quartz-cement kinetics from Walderhaug (1996). No other authigenic cements in phase 1.

name: chalk
phi0_source: literature: Sclater & Christie (1980) JGR 85; same built-in value as lithology.py
phi_r_source: assumed: mechanical-only chalk retains high porosity until chemical compaction / pressure solution (not modelled in phase 1; see Croizé et al. 2013 review / Schneider et al. 1996 viscoplastic term)
beta_1_MPa_source: assumed: softer mechanical compaction than shale so that chemical compaction (future work) can do the remaining porosity loss
grain_size_m_source: assumed: nannofossil micrite scale (~5 μm); not used for chalk permeability (see Mortensen/Fabricius note)
f_quartz_source: assumed: little detrital quartz in chalk
f_clay_source: assumed: chalk is not a mudstone; a low CF is used only if the mudstone law is ever applied to this end-member
coat_source: assumed: almost no clean quartz surface available for Walderhaug quartz cement
friction_deg_source: literature: typical friction angle for chalk (geotechnical range; not measured here)
note: Carbonate pressure solution is not applied in phase 1; chalk porosity here is mechanical plus whatever tiny quartz cement the kinetics produce. Permeability uses Kozeny k=c φ^3/S^2 (Mortensen et al. 1998; Fabricius 2007) with c=0.25 and a literature-prior BET surface of 2.0 m2/g (Fabricius 2007 North Sea chalk range; not a well measurement).
